clue.text: Father has the lead in this dance

parts.note: Pa is a familiar word for father
the van is the leading part, as in 'in the van' of an army

explanation.surface: A dad takes the leading role in a dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has' is a link word joining the two pieces. The PAVAN is a stately old court dance, also spelt pavane.
explanation.definitionFit: A stately sixteenth-century processional court dance carries this name.

clue.text: Someone competent of good appearance

parts.note: a person is someone
able means competent

explanation.surface: A capable person who also looks good.
explanation.definitionFit: Personable describes someone pleasant in looks and manner, attractive.

clue.text: Lunchtime paper ?

parts.note: suggests a midday newspaper, but means a paper token handed over to pay for a meal

explanation.surface: A newspaper read over lunch.
explanation.walkthrough: Luncheon vouchers were paper tokens British employers gave staff to pay for lunch.
explanation.definitionFit: A paper coupon exchanged for goods, as in the old British luncheon tokens.

clue.text: Heavens ! How low can you get ?

definitions.text: Heavens ! How low can you get ?

parts.words: Heavens ! How low can you get ?
parts.note: sounds like an exclamation of shock at someone's behaviour, but asks for the lowest point of the celestial sphere

explanation.surface: Someone is appalled at a shameful act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heavens!' looks like an exclamation, but it points to astronomy: the point of the heavens directly below the observer, opposite the zenith.
explanation.definitionFit: The lowest point, astronomically the spot in the celestial sphere directly underfoot.

clue.text: Set fire to one outhouse -polished it off ?

parts.note: to burn something is to set fire to it
the Roman numeral I stands for one
a shed is a small outbuilding

explanation.surface: Someone torches a garden shed, and the question mark asks whether that finished it off.
explanation.walkthrough: The trailing 'it off?' is surface play: burning down the shed 'polished it off', i.e. destroyed it, while 'polished' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To burnish metal is to rub it until it shines, so burnished means polished bright.

clue.text: Cry of pain in uncovered carriage

indicators.note: in says the cry goes inside the word for uncovered

parts.note: bare means uncovered
ouch is what you cry when hurt

explanation.surface: Someone yelps in an open-topped carriage.
explanation.definitionFit: A barouche is a four-wheeled horse-drawn coach with a folding hood.

clue.text: Pierce with difficulty cook's well-kept secret

indicators.note: with difficulty suggests the letters are forced into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A chef's guarded method can be penetrated only with effort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pierce' looks like a verb, but it is the anagram fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A chef's prized instructions for a dish are often closely guarded.

clue.text: Cape Town for the British !

explanation.surface: Cape Town, the South African city, claimed by Britain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cape Town' is two words doing separate jobs. An Inverness cape is a sleeveless cloak; Inverness is a town in the Scottish Highlands.
explanation.definitionFit: A sleeveless cloak with a cape over the shoulders is named after a Highland town, and the town is the other sense.

clue.text: My hat ! Coarse food to the Health Officer ? Turn it up !

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning something up means the whole string is written from bottom to top

parts.note: grub is slang for plain food
MOH stands for Medical Officer of Health

explanation.surface: An exclamation at rough food served to an official, who tells it to stop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn it up!' sounds like British slang for 'stop it', but reverses GRUB + MOH to give HOM + BURG. 'My hat!' sounds like surprise but defines a felt hat.
explanation.definitionFit: A Homburg is a man's felt hat with a dented crown and curled brim.

clue.text: Sound as a bell, but his nose was shiny

explanation.surface: Someone is perfectly healthy, though his nose glows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound as a bell' looks like the idiom for fit and well. Edward Lear wrote the nonsense poem 'The Dong with a Luminous Nose'.
explanation.definitionFit: The deep ring of a bell; and Edward Lear's nonsense creature with a glowing nose.

clue.text: Players' circuit more like the Globe ?

explanation.surface: Actors tour while the Globe theatre looks ever more circular.
explanation.walkthrough: In the British bat-and-ball game rounders, a player who runs a full circuit of the bases scores a rounder. The Globe is the round Shakespearean theatre, and also the earth.
explanation.definitionFit: A full run of the bases in the game of rounders scores one; and the comparative of round, more spherical like a globe.

clue.text: Club retainer used to drag his wife along

definitions.text: Club retainer used to drag his wife along

parts.words: Club retainer used to drag his wife along
parts.note: reads like a servant at a gentlemen's club, but describes the cartoon prehistoric man who holds a club and hauls his mate by the hair

explanation.surface: A club's servant is employed to haul a member's wife along.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Club' suggests a gentlemen's club and 'retainer' a servant, but the club is a wooden cudgel and the retainer is the one holding it.
explanation.definitionFit: The cartoon picture of a Stone Age man shows him gripping a cudgel and dragging his woman by the hair.

clue.text: Back to her ? It's not the same

indicators.note: Back tells us the little word to is written backwards

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Returning to a woman, someone remarks that things have changed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back to her?' reads as a question about returning to a woman; 'Back' is the reversal signal working on the little word that follows it.
explanation.definitionFit: Something different or distinct from the one already mentioned is so described.

clue.text: Shoe slit. Blow !

parts.note: the upper is the part of a shoe above the sole
a cut is a slit

explanation.surface: Someone discovers a gash in a shoe and swears.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blow!' looks like an exclamation of annoyance at the damaged shoe, but it is the definition: a punch.
explanation.definitionFit: A boxer's upward punch to the chin is a classic knockout blow.

clue.text: Calling for spirits — seeing what's in store for you

definitions.text: seeing what's in store for you

explanation.surface: Someone summons ghosts while telling a fortune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Calling for spirits' sounds like ordering drinks; it means summoning the dead.
explanation.definitionFit: Summoning the dead and foretelling the future by such communion are both meanings of this black art.

clue.text: Like a balloon, three sheets in the wind ?

parts.note: wind is moving air
'three sheets in the wind' means drunk, and tight is slang for drunk

explanation.surface: A drunk is as inflated as a balloon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Three sheets in the wind' is an idiom for drunk, but the phrase is split into two pieces, with 'in' a link word; the balloon is sealed tight.
explanation.definitionFit: A balloon must be sealed so no gas leaks out.

clue.text: Shows how one writes about an accountant

indicators.note: about says the writing word surrounds the accountant

parts.note: to indite is to compose or write
CA is a chartered accountant

explanation.surface: An explanation of how a person writes about an accountant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'how one' is a link phrase. Indite is an old, formal verb for composing a letter or poem.
explanation.definitionFit: To indicate something is to point it out or make it plain.

clue.text: Darwin's crafty dog

explanation.surface: Charles Darwin owned a cunning hound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crafty' is not cunning: it means 'craft', a vessel. HMS Beagle was the ship on which Darwin sailed round the world.
explanation.definitionFit: The naval ship that carried the naturalist on his voyage bore this name; and a small hound bred for hunting hares.

clue.text: Dab discovered far below the surface

parts.note: a dab hand is an expert, a pro
found means discovered

explanation.surface: A dab, the flatfish, is found deep under the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dab' suggests the flatfish living on the seabed, but stands for an expert.
explanation.definitionFit: Profound literally means very deep, reaching to great depth.

clue.text: Gulliver found an old timer having trouble in Balnibarbi

parts.note: an old lag is a convict who has served time, so a lag is an old timer
ado means fuss or trouble

explanation.surface: Swift's traveller meets a struggling old man in a fictional land.
explanation.walkthrough: LAGADO is the capital of Balnibarbi in Gulliver's Travels, home of the absurd Academy. An old lag is British slang for a veteran prisoner.
explanation.definitionFit: Swift's satire names the capital city of that flying-island kingdom, visited by the hero on his third voyage.

clue.text: Forbidding, one to make a face

parts.note: grim means forbidding or stern
an ace counts as one in cards

explanation.surface: A stern person pulls a face.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to make a' is a link phrase; a grimace is the face one makes.
explanation.definitionFit: A twisted expression of pain or disgust pulled with the features.

clue.text: Inside man

parts.note: an insider in a heist, but read literally a man who is 'inside', slang for being in jail

explanation.definitionFit: Someone held in jail is said to be inside.

clue.text: Game for the fishermen's dance?

parts.note: fishermen use a net
a ball is a formal dance

explanation.surface: Is there a game suited to a fishermen's ball?
explanation.walkthrough: 'for the' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: A team sport where goals are scored by throwing through a high hoop.

clue.text: Flexible part of the gun-carriage

explanation.surface: A bendy component of a gun's carriage.
explanation.walkthrough: A limber is the detachable two-wheeled front section that towed a field gun.
explanation.definitionFit: Supple and lithe; also the detachable front of a field-gun carriage holding ammunition.

clue.text: What destructive mice get up to with the fish!

definitions.text: What destructive mice get up to with the fish!

indicators.note: destructive suggests the letters of the creatures are torn apart and rebuilt

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Wrecking rodents make trouble with the fish.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of MICE and FISH together are rearranged; the whole clue also describes the result.
explanation.definitionFit: Destructive rodents cause harm and naughty trouble, which is the sense of the word.

clue.text: Some caused a tumult at the base-line

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A disturbance broke out on the tennis base line.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run from causeD A TUMult.
explanation.definitionFit: A surveyor's reference line from which heights are measured is a datum line, a base line.

clue.text: These birds went to the same parties

parts.note: do is short for ditto, meaning the same
dos are parties

explanation.surface: Birds attending identical parties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'went to' are link words, with a nod to the birds being long gone.
explanation.definitionFit: Flightless extinct pigeons from Mauritius.

clue.text: Border instrument coming up

indicators.note: in a down clue coming up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: a tuba is a brass instrument

explanation.surface: A Border bagpiper's instrument advancing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming up' reverses TUBA. 'Border' looks like the Scottish Borders but is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To abut is to adjoin or share a boundary with.

clue.text: Have a hand in this presently for charity

definitions.text: Have a hand in this presently for charity

parts.words: Have a hand in this presently for charity
parts.note: 'have a hand in' suggests being involved, but literally means plunging your hand into a container of bran at a fete

explanation.surface: Someone is urged to get involved soon in a charity project.
explanation.walkthrough: A bran tub is a British fete game: a tub of bran with prizes buried in it, which you dip a hand into for a small fee that goes to charity.
explanation.definitionFit: A lucky-dip barrel at a fundraising fete has wrapped prizes buried in husks for players to grope for.

clue.text: One's bonds may be, but not that oven-ready bird!

definitions.text: One's bonds may be, but not that oven-ready bird!

parts.words: One's bonds may be, but not that oven-ready bird!
parts.note: a premium bond not yet picked in the prize draw is in this state, whereas a bird ready for roasting has had its innards removed

explanation.surface: A remark comparing a person's savings bonds with a chicken ready to roast.
explanation.walkthrough: Premium Bonds are British savings bonds entered into a monthly prize draw. A bird is 'drawn' when gutted, so an oven-ready one is not in the opposite state.
explanation.definitionFit: Not picked in a prize ballot, and of poultry, still with its entrails in.

clue.text: Walk about certain to be highly esteemed

indicators.note: about says the word for walk goes round the word for certain

parts.note: to tread is to walk
sure means certain

explanation.surface: Strolling around confident of being greatly admired.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Something treasured is cherished and valued greatly.

clue.text: Ill-tempered vehicle

explanation.definitionFit: Moody and resentful; also a light two-wheeled one-seat cart used in harness racing.
